title: How do two heights compare on a zoomed chart?
description: A chart's vertical line starts at one hundred and forty five centimetres, and two markers sit at one hundred and sixty five and one hundred and fifty five. Their lengths from the line are twenty and ten, yet the true heights are almost the same. Keeko doubts this and thinks the longer marker is twice as tall.
teaching_notes: One idea: when a chart's line does not start at zero, lengths no longer compare in the ratio of the heights, so read the values. Watch for students who compare the lengths of markers as if they were the heights.

source: On a chart whose axis starts at 145 cm, one marker sits at 1
video_script.why: The child can read values on a line and now notices where the line starts before comparing lengths.
video_script.substitution: A marker's length above a zoomed line shows only the part above the starting value.
video_script.anchor: The book's chart of average heights of nineteen year olds in different countries, its vertical line starting at 145 cm, with two markers at 165 cm and 155 cm
video_script.wrong_answer: the first marker is twice as tall as the second
video_script.wrong_move: Compares the lengths above the zoomed starting line as if they were the heights, forgetting the first one hundred and forty five centimetres.
video_script.payoff_line: The first marker is two times as long, but only a little taller.

final_answer.spoken: two times as long, but the true ratio is about one point zero six

maths_rules: the vertical line starts at 145 cm, not at 0
length of the first marker above the line: 165 - 145 = 20
length of the second marker above the line: 155 - 145 = 10
ratio of the true heights: 165 ÷ 155 = 1.0645, about 1.06
(165 - 155) ÷ 155 = 0.0645, so the first is about 6 percent taller
lengths compare as 20 to 10 but the heights compare as 165 to 155
video_script.design: One chart, two markers. A strip of 145 cm hidden under each marker fills in when the doubt is broken.
open_questions: The markers at 165 cm and 155 cm are the worklist's example values; the book only says its chart's vertical line starts at 145 cm.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a chart from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It shows the average heights of nineteen year olds in different countries.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Its vertical line starts at one hundred and forty five centimetres, not at zero.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Two markers sit at one hundred and sixty five and one hundred and fifty five centimetres.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>How do the lengths of the markers compare, and how do their true heights compare?

beats.on_screen: the chart and the question stay on the board

marks.m1: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the vertical line with its lowest mark 145 cm; a bracket from the line up to a marker shows its length

marks.m1: an ordinary line starting at 0 flashes and fades
marks.m2: the line of the chart shows 145 at the bottom
marks.m3: a bracket measures a marker from the starting line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>On most charts the vertical line starts at zero.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Here the line starts at one hundred and forty five instead.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A marker's length is measured from that starting line, not from zero.

beats.on_screen: Given: line starts at 145 cm; markers at 165 cm and 155 cm
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the vertical line starts at one hundred and forty five centimetres.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One marker is at one hundred and sixty five and the other at one hundred and fifty five.

beats.on_screen: To find: compare the lengths; compare the true heights

marks.m1: the two questions are written one under the other

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to compare the lengths of the markers, and then compare their true heights.

beats.on_screen: length of first marker = 165 - 145 = 20; length of second marker = 155 - 145 = 10

marks.m1: the rule length = height - 145 is written
marks.m2: 165 - 145 appears and the first bracket is drawn
marks.m3: 155 - 145 appears and the second bracket is drawn

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find each length above the starting line. A length is measured from that line.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For the first marker, one hundred and sixty five take away one hundred and forty five is twenty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>For the second marker, one hundred and fifty five take away one hundred and forty five is ten.

marks.m2: the first bracket is shown as two copies of the second

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, divide the longer length by the shorter one, twenty divided by ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The first marker is two times as long as the second.

beats.on_screen: compare the true heights: 165 ÷ 155, a little more than 1

marks.m2: the two full heights from zero are drawn side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, divide the true heights the same way. Heights are measured from zero. We divide one hundred and sixty five by one hundred and fifty five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That is only a little more than one, so the heights are close.

beats.on_screen: Answer: lengths 2 times; heights 165 ÷ 155 ≈ 1.06, about 6 percent taller
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The first marker is two times as long, but only a little taller.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The true heights divide to about one point zero six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That is only about six percent taller than the second marker.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the chart
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's doubt: the first marker is twice as tall; it is struck through as a 145 cm strip fills in under each marker

marks.m1: the doubt appears as a bubble
marks.m2: the strip of 145 cm fills in under each marker and the bubble is struck through
marks.m3: the words read the values appear

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the first marker is twice as tall as the second. Its length is twice as long.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But each length leaves out the first one hundred and forty five centimetres of the height.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Lengths on a zoomed line do not compare the true heights. Read the values on the line, not the lengths.
